newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: China's Sinochem Singapore listing plan put on ice.
newsitem.headline: China's Sinochem Singapore listing plan put on ice.

text.p: China's state trading company, China National Chemicals Import & Export Corp (SINOCHEM) has put plans to list on the Stock Exchange of Singapore (SES) on ice, company officials said on Thursday.

"It has been postponed indefinitely," a senior Beijing-based SINOCHEM official, who declined to be identified, told Reuters. SINOCHEM said in 1995 it planned to list in Singapore, initially with its Singapore-incorporated Sinochem Asia Holdings, by mid-1996.
But the listing has been delayed several times even though the Stock Echange of Singapore (SES) and China's Securities Regulatory Commission has approved the plan.
The Company has given no reason for the delays gave no reasons for the delays and declined comment on the indefinite postponement.
But one Chinese source said SINOCHEM decided to put the move on ice because it was asked to list on Singapore's newer foreign board instead of the more established main board.
A Singapore Stock Exchange spokesman declined comment.

"The main reason for the pull out is because SES had given approval for the company to list on the foreign board while it wants to listed on the mainboard," said the source. "And SINOCHEM was concern about the liquidity on the foreign board." The SES foreign board was created to attract foreign companies, particularly infrastructure companies, to list in Singapore. Their shares have to be denominated in a foreign currency.
The requirements for a listing on the foreign board are generally less stringent than those for the main board but so far only one company, CM Telecom, has listed on the foreign board.
However, Singapore corporate finance advisers said they doubted liquidity was a problem in the SINOCHEM case.

"Liquidity should not be an issue. Whether SINOCHEM lists on the foreign or main board, it should do well based on its fundamentals and the company name," said a local banker familiar with Chinese companies seeking a listing in Singapore.
Another banking source said SINOCHEM would probably have problems meeting the requirements for a Singapore dollar listing on the SES mainboard since most of its sales are generated outside Singapore.
SINOCHEM trades an array of commodities from oil to steel and even garments and is one of China's premier importers and exporters of crude oil and refined oil product.
Oil traders in Singapore said SINOCHEM's financial performance in recent years might have been affected as it has had problems in collecting payments from customers.

"This is a very serious problem. Whenever international oil prices rise sharply, Chinese endusers cannot pay. Nothing can be done about it and the bottom line will be affected," said an oil trader with a Chinese company.
The Chinese sources in Beijing also dismissed suggestions that SINOCHEM's listing plans were suspended because it did not get the go-ahead from China's Securities Regulatory Commission (CSRC).
All overseas listings of foreign subsidiaries of China's state-owned companies must have CSRC's approval.
